blocks.text: 在过去一个月的大部分时间里，我交谈和关注的许多网络安全专家发帖时都显得非常恐惧。许多人一直在警告一场由AI驱动的“黑天鹅”事件，对突然发现的大量漏洞感到警觉，也对AI代理和大型语言模型在发现和利用此前未知漏洞方面显而易见的强大能力感到不安。

blocks.text: 发生的事情如此之多、如此之快，以至于对我——一个报道和编辑安全与黑客相关新闻已有十年的人来说——都难以完全理解正在发生什么、对接下来可能发生什么有清晰判断，或预测这将走向何方。而我认为，在我写下这些的时候，这大体上就是我们目前的处境。

blocks.text: 但已经很清楚的是，广义上的人工智能已经从根本上改变了攻击性黑客行为和防御性网络安全。这并不是因为人工智能有了意识，也不是因为人类失去了对它的控制，也不是因为出现了“流氓智能体”的“蜂群”，而是因为人工智能正在证明一件我们一直都知道的事：运行互联网、我们的设备、我们的账户以及我们生活的许多软件都是脆弱的、过时的，或者存在人类从未注意到的安全漏洞，或者是由某家公司某个人安装的，而那个人六年前就离开了公司，岗位已经换了四次，现在没人知道怎么找到他，也不知道怎么更新它。这并不意味着在人工智能帮助下发现的所有漏洞都是显而易见或微不足道的；熟练的黑客和研究人员借助人工智能工具，似乎在发现漏洞方面比单靠人类更强。但关键在于，人工智能和大语言模型让对互联网进行本质上的暴力破解变得极其容易；如果把每一款软件都比作一扇门，人工智能让转动每一扇门把手、看看它是否没锁变得异常简单，即便是人类从未真正费心尝试打开的建筑也不例外。我们正以惊人的速度认识到，不仅有些锁很容易撬开，在某些情况下门是大敞的，或者墙上有个大洞。最近一连串有人用人工智能入侵自己的物联网设备来运行新软件的事件表明，在某些情况下，实际上不需要任何专业知识就能用人工智能入侵某些东西。

blocks.text: 在解释 PHP 漏洞发现的博客文章中，OpenAI 表示这些发现凸显了“人工智能如何能发现具有互联网规模影响的安全漏洞，但同样的能力也能帮助攻击者快速开发攻击工具和漏洞利用程序”。OpenAI 基本上主张，它是以合乎伦理的方式完成所有这些研究的，并且其发现开启了一个“防御者窗口”，让政府和关键基础设施能够为该漏洞的披露做好准备。“研究人员发现漏洞，以合乎伦理的方式向公司披露，公司修复它”是网络安全领域的首选做法，但人工智能正在缩短这一切的窗口期，正引导更多人以更低的门槛做更多的研究，并让漏洞发现和漏洞修复都变得快得多。至于这些修复是否真的会被各个公司更快地部署，则是另一个复杂得多的问题。在许多情况下，答案很可能是：不会。

blocks.text: AI 也让这一切变得更加难以预测。安全公司 Chainguard 因违反 PHP 漏洞披露的禁令而受到批评，因为它在漏洞被正式披露前数小时就发布了修复方案。批评者包括 PHP 基金会表示，这可能让攻击者在网站所有者有机会保护其系统之前就弄清楚如何利用这些问题。Chainguard 首席执行官 Dan Lorenc 在 LinkedIn 的一篇帖子中表示，他的公司通过向前沿 AI 模型输入“find bad vulnerabilities in PHP”独立发现了同样的漏洞。与此同时，亚马逊表示，它在官方披露之前就看到了漏洞利用尝试。这些事实引发了疑问：这个漏洞是否异常容易发现；最初发现这些漏洞的 AI 模型是否以某种方式将这些信息纳入了模型，从而使其他人更容易发现；还是披露流程相关的某个人在过程中泄露了信息。任何一种可能都令人担忧。

blocks.text: 正如The Atlantic 已经指出的那样，PHP2Shell 最大的影响之一可能是：许多历史网站无法或不会更新，可能被主动下线，最终可能被黑客入侵，并且可能再也无法恢复。链接失效的情况可能极其严重，大量历史可能就此丢失。

blocks.alt: AI Is Changing Everything About Hacking. No One Knows What Happens Next

blocks.text: For much of the last month, many of the cybersecurity experts I talk to and follow have been posting like they are very scared. Many have been warning of an AI-powered “Black Swan” event, have been alarmed by the number of vulnerabilities suddenly discovered, and of the apparent power of AI agents and large language models more broadly to find and exploit previously unknown bugs.

inlines.text: For much of the last month, many of the cybersecurity experts I talk to and follow have been posting like they are very scared. Many have been warning of an AI-powered “Black Swan” event, have been alarmed by the number of vulnerabilities suddenly discovered, and of the apparent power of AI agents and large language models more broadly to find and exploit previously unknown bugs.

blocks.text: The rhetoric has ranged from worried-but-measured (things are about to get weird), to run-of-the-mill advice like update your software and make sure you have two-factor authentication on, to vagueposting about AI-powered attacks, to things like ‘the internet was nice while it lasted,’ to outright prepper-level terror.

blocks.text: To give you a sense of what I’m seeing, Matthew Green, a Johns Hopkins professor and one of the most respected cryptographers in the world, posted “we’re in the part of the movie where you need to throw whatever you can in the path of the zombies and hope it slows them down,” and “so many people discovering that the whole Internet is dry tinder and the only thing keeping it from burning is the fact that teenagers haven’t found the matches yet,” Green is alluding to the fact that hackers and researchers driving AI tools and agents are getting better at finding and exploiting all sorts of bugs in important systems. I’ve also seen numerous AI employees, as mentioned, go full prepper, suggesting people pull money out of their bank accounts, disconnect from the internet, purchase shelf-stable food, hoard water, put money in gold and cash, and purchase hand-crank emergency radios.

blocks.text: And all those posts came before people using AI-powered tools found vulnerabilities in PHP, the programming language that powers much of the internet. In the last few days, major vulnerabilities or issues have been found in eMudhra (an Indian entity that provides website security certificates), Node.js (an alternative to PHP), Gitlab (a software development platform), Plex (media server software), Railway (a cloud provider), OpenCode (a coding agent platform), and several other companies and services, though, rightfully, none of these has gotten as much attention as the vulnerabilities in PHP, called PHP2Shell, which researchers from Wiz, Calif, and OpenAI discovered using AI.

blocks.text: Matthew Prince, the CEO of Cloudflare, a service that has wide insight into the general health of the internet, posted, “In the 10 hours before [PHP2Shell] was publicly announced, across the Cloudflare network we saw thousands of attempts to exploit it. That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now.”

blocks.text: So much is happening, and so quickly, that it has been difficult for me — someone who has been reporting and editing stories on security and hacking for a decade — to fully understand what’s going on, to have a sense of what could happen next, or predict where this is going. And I think that that is largely where we are at the moment, as I am writing this.

blocks.text: But it has become clear that AI, broadly defined, has fundamentally changed both offensive hacking and defensive cybersecurity. This is not because AI has become sentient or because human beings have lost control of it or because of “swarms” of “rogue agents,” but because AI is proving something that we have always known: much of the software that runs the internet, our devices, our accounts, and our lives is vulnerable, or out of date, or has security flaws that human beings never noticed, or was installed by someone at a company who left the company six years ago and has been replaced four times and no one knows how to find them now or how to update it. This doesn’t mean that all of the vulnerabilities that have been found with the help of AI have been obvious or trivial; skilled hackers and researchers, driving AI tools, seem to be better than humans alone at finding vulnerabilities. But, critically, AI and large language models have made it extremely easy to essentially brute force the internet; if every piece of software is a door, AI makes it exceptionally easy to turn turn the knobs of every door to see if it’s unlocked, even on buildings that human beings had never really bothered to try to open. What we are learning at an alarmingly fast pace is that not only are some of the locks easy to pick, in some cases the door is wide open or there’s a giant hole in the wall. The recent spate of people using AI to hack their internet of things devices to run new software shows that, in some cases, it takes essentially no expertise to actually use AI to hack something.

blocks.text: Meanwhile, we've seen the rise of "abliterated" AI models that are designed to not say no and open weights models that can be used for pentesting and potentially offensive hacks without the guardrails that exist in many off-the-shelf commercial models.

blocks.text: In a blog post explaining the PHP vulnerability discovery, OpenAI said the findings highlight “how AI can uncover security flaws with internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits.” OpenAI basically argues that it did all of this research ethically, and that its discovery opened a “Defender’s Window” that allowed governments and critical infrastructure to prepare for the disclosure of the bug. ‘Researcher finds bug, ethically discloses it to company, company fixes it’ is the preferred course of action in cybersecurity, but AI is shortening the window for all of this, is leading more people to do more research more easily, and is making both bug finding and bug fixing much faster. Whether those fixes are actually deployed by individual companies any faster is another, much more complicated question. The answer in many cases is, probably, no.

blocks.text: AI is also making all of this much more unpredictable. The security company Chainguard was criticized for breaking the embargo on the PHP vulnerability disclosure because it posted fixes for the vulnerabilities several hours before it was officially disclosed. Critics, including the PHP Foundation, said this could have let attackers figure out how to exploit the issues before website owners had a chance to protect their systems. In a LinkedIn post, Chainguard CEO Dan Lorenc said that his company independently found the same bugs by typing “find bad vulnerabilities in PHP” into a frontier AI model. Amazon, meanwhile, said that it saw exploit attempts before the official disclosure. These facts raise questions about whether the bug was exceptionally easy to find, whether the AI models that originally found the vulnerabilities incorporated that information into the model somehow therefore making it easier for someone else to find, or whether there was a leak along the way from someone connected to the disclosure process. Any option is concerning.

blocks.text: After the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities were discovered, some infosec experts started calling this “Black October,” and highlighted the fact that the National Security Agency, the Prime Minister of Japan, and various governments around the world told people to patch their websites and services immediately, and to take down services that couldn’t be patched. 4chan, several Wikimedia services, and Archive.org were all temporarily taken offline so that they could be updated.

blocks.text: As The Atlantic has already suggested, one of the biggest impacts of PHP2Shell could be the fact that many historic websites can’t or won’t be updated, may be proactively pulled offline, might eventually be hacked, and might never come back. The link rot could be horrendous, and a lot of history could be lost.

blocks.text: For such a high-profile incident, most of the actual impacts thus far have been related to the proactive patching or removal of potentially insecure websites, and we have not seen immediate, widespread exploitation of the bug. Various low-effort, LLM-developed exploits have been dropped online; many of them will not work. A blog post called “There isn’t an easy exploit for this PHP vulnerability,” written by Elias Taylor, quickly went viral and was dissected on Hacker News, especially by people pointing out that the website eliastaylor.com had been recently registered and that it wasn’t clear who Elias Taylor was. 404 Media reached Taylor by Signal; he said “I am real and on a delayed train.”

But patch your servers, it’s still a vulnerability. Please do not paraphrase me as saying ‘there is no vulnerability’ for any reason. There is, and people should patch.”

blocks.text: Dan Guido, the CEO of Trail of Bits, a well-respected cybersecurity company that partners with OpenAI on the Patch the Planet initiative, posted that his company had created “a working exploit,” and that “Will Tan built it in 1 day with Codex, drawing on ~10 years of system security and vulnerability research. AI accelerates exploit development. Knowing how to turn a bug into a shell still takes expertise. AI makes that expertise more productive.”

blocks.text: It remains unclear, at the moment, what the ultimate impact of all of this is going to be, or where we’ll be in one hour, one week, one year, or 10 years. But AI is changing how cybersecurity and hacking works. It is making finding and exploiting bugs faster and easier. We’re about to find out how insecure the internet really is.
